title: Form follows growth rates in large organisms but not in minute ones

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Form follows growth rates in large organisms but not in minute ones

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Large and small organisms differ in kind in how form arises: in large organisms form is the direct result of unequal growth rates in different directions, but in minute organisms and individual cells intermolecular forces outweigh gravity and form is not simply correlated with growth.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: But it is by no means true that form and growth are in this direct and simple fashion correlative or complementary in the case of minute portions of living matter.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter II, “On Magnitude”; topic “Surface tension rules small organisms”. Scope: large multicellular organisms versus small organisms and individual cells

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch02-14: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.46

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Existing time-lapse imaging can test the growth-form relation in exemplar systems. The asserted categorical scale split requires substantial modern interpretation and broad matched data that do not currently exist.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Infer directional growth fields from time-lapse imaging and test whether they predict shape change in large organisms but fail in minute organisms, where measured cortical or interfacial forces should instead predict form. Cross-scale predictive comparisons would support or refute the proposed dichotomy.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Growth and active molecular forces jointly determine form at both scales.

Large and minute lack a stated threshold.

Comparable force and growth fields are rarely available.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The large-versus-minute contrast is testable in principle with growth maps, and some public images and ontogenetic scans exist. They do not jointly cover rates and form across the two regimes, and for multicellular growth the rate-ratio account is close to a kinematic identity. Discriminating it from patterning, migration, and mechanical deformation needs data that are still mostly in individual studies.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For large organisms, test whether the change in external shape equals the integral of directional growth rates. For cells and minute organisms, test whether shape is uncorrelated with those rates once surface or intermolecular forces are accounted for. A large organism whose form changed mainly by migration or cell death without anisotropic growth would count against the first clause.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Anisotropic growth can be a redescription of shape change, which weakens the contrast with rivals.

Directional growth rates and shape are seldom in the same public file.
